rv.q: This is one rock-solid company of dancin’ fools.
Rightfully so, because 'Dancin'' is as metal as musical theater gets.
This is a show hell-bent on making sure that you have fun, laughs, good times at any cost.

That truth surely dances around your head at 'Bob Fosse’s Dancin’,' the fascinating, if deeply conflicted, new Broadway revival of the hit 1978 revue 'Dancin’.' It’s now more tightly branded around its famous, or infamous, choreographer and restaged at the Theatre by Wayne Cilento, an orig...
The revival of Bob Fosse's 'Dancin'' is a slick, stylish celebration of the choreographer's distinctive vocabulary, even if it doesn't quite capture the electric atmosphere of the original.
The show is a joy every time it puts down its ax.

The show is essentially a jukebox musical built around Fosse's choreographic legacy, but it lacks the narrative drive or thematic coherence that might give it more lasting impact beyond the undeniable pleasure of watching skilled dancers execute Fosse's inimitable moves.
The show is a showcase for some excellent dancers, but it feels more like a museum piece than a living, breathing work of theater.
“Unhappily, the first revival of Fosse’s all-dance, plotless revue ... does not represent the man at his most inspired...
Bob Fosse's Dancin' doesn't just make old moves fresh — it makes us feel like we're discovering Fosse anew.
Cilento sought to update the show and introduce Bob Fosse to a new generation — and he mostly succeeds.
The heart, soul, and irrepressible spirit of Bob Fosse's Dancin', which just opened in a burst of sparkle and joy at Broadway's Theatre, is best embodied in the curtain call.
If you want to see some of the best triple-threats in the biz, head on over to experience some true Fosse magic.
But there are dozens of sometimes dazzling dances performed by twenty-two gorgeously talented and hard-working cast members.
Here, the dancers are not just center stage, but they are also named in big letters as they come out individually to bow.
There’s a smug irony to this presentation of Americana that’s especially unwarranted.
What might she have thought of this dubious enterprise?
This new incarnation feels like an advanced class in Fosse in which all the students have learned how the pronounce well enough for us to understand but they still have a heavy accent.

Bob Fosse’s Dancin’ may not be perfect, but if you want two hours of nearly nonstop, essentially nonverbal demonstrations of the beauty, power, and expressiveness of Broadway dancing as conceived by one of its foremost creative geniuses, this is the moment.
Cilento’s exceptional reimagining manifests how Fosse stylized the art form toward an apotheosis of vibrance, sexiness, rigor and grace.
But when Dancin’ dances, it’s unstoppable.
Others may want to shuffle off to another this season’s many new Broadway offerings.
